In the Tempelfjorden and Dicksonland areas the rocks studied were characterized by a very small dip that did not exceed 10ë. A different tectonic situation is found in the Trygghamna area where the beds are steeply (60±85ë) inclined towards NEE (KSF) or NE (Vardebukta Fm.) direction. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of specimens was measured using spinner and cryo- genic magnetometers. Some pilot samples were sub- jected to an alternating ®eld demagnetization ex- periment. Because this method was not effective, the majority of the sample set has been subjected to step- wise thermal demagnetization in a m-metal shielded oven, which reduced the ambient ®eld close to a few nT. After each thermal demagnetization level the magnetic susceptibility signal was monitored. Least- square line ®t methods, as presented by Kirschvink [16], were used to calculate the components of NRM and their unblocking temperature spectra. Thermo- magnetic analysis and isothermal remanent magne- tization (IRM) acquisition were used to determine the nature of magnetic carriers. For some samples, hysteresis loops were also determined. 4. Results of paleomagnetic analysis Only a small subset of the samples yielded well- de®ned, antipodal directions of presumed Permian± Triassic age that were useful for paleopole calcu- lations; however, about half of the samples yielded polarity indications. During thermal demagnetiza- tion between 380ëC and 435ëC, an abrupt increase of magnetic susceptibility was observed in the bulk of samples, and their demagnetization was terminated at this point. In many samples from all sections only one distinct component `A' with very steep, posi- tive inclination (75±90ë) was isolated (Fig. 3a). This component results most probably from a widespread remagnetization that affected Spitsbergen in Ceno- zoic time (e.g. [17]). Some samples from a narrow tectonic zone which cuts the Trygghamna section also contain steep component `A', but with a nega- tive inclination (Fig. 3a, sample th52). In this tec- tonic zone, the NRM intensities were about an order of magnitude higher than those in the remagnetized samples with a positive inclination. About 50% of the samples also revealed a compo- nent `B' with moderate angles of negative or positive inclination. Introduction The post-Permian paleotectonic position of Spits- bergen is still a matter of a debate. Rowley and Lottes [1] considered Svalbard to be a separate mi- croplate during the Mesozoic. Malod and Mauffret [2] hypothesized paleo-north to south rifting be- tween Spitsbergen and Norway. As remarked by Van der V oo [3], such a solution implies that pre-rifting Spitsbergen paleomagnetic poles would not be valid for Stable Europe. Devonian and Early Carbonif- erous poles from Spitsbergen [4,5] ®t well on the Baltic apparent polar wander path (APWP), but Late Carboniferous±Permian poles [6,7] deviate from that APWP. It should be stressed, how- ever, that in many paleotectonic maps (e.g. [8]) such post-Caledonian movement of Spitsbergen relative to the European plate has not been taken into account. We present Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic results from Sikhote Alin to investigate the tectonic evolution of the marginal area since the Late Cretaceous. Geological setting and sampling The basement of the Sikhote Alin mountain range consists mainly of a Late Jurassic accretionary complex and Early Cretaceous turbidites. The basement is cut by a large sinistral fault trending NE-SW (central Sikhote Alin fault). Finally, 199 8±2M aM i n t o dykes of west-northwest to northwest trend, identical in age to the 1998 M a±2M aP u r t u n i qophiolite of the Cape Smith Belt, have a paleopole at 38°N, 174°E. The similarity of paleopoles for the ca. 2.23–2.21 Ga Maguire dykes of the Minto block, Senneterre dykes of the southern Superior, and Nipissing sills of the Southern Province demonstrates that these regions were in their present relative latitudes and orientations at that time. . Following the major tectonic activity, metamorphism, and plutonism at ca. 2.7 Ga, the Minto block cooled to record ca. 2.5 Ga K–Ar mica dates. It was transected by several swarms of diabase dykes (Fig. 1), some of which are likely linked to Paleoproterozoic rifting events (ca. 2.2–2.0 Ga) at the margins of the Superior Province. Only minor deforma - tion and retrogression of the Superior craton is associated with subsequent (ca. 1.8 Ga) compressional orogeny in the New Quebec and Ungava orogens. In this study, the Ptarmigan, Maguire, Klotz, and Minto dyke swarms (Fig. 1) are defined on the basis of their U–Pb geochronology, paleomagnetism, petrographic characteris- tics, and trend. The extent of Ptarmigan, Maguire, and Minto swarms is poorly defined because the dykes are not readily traceable on aeromagnetic maps. Dykes of the Klotz swarm are also not evident on aeromagnetic maps, but can be easily traced on aerial photographs. The 2505 Ma Ptarmigan swarm consists of only a few dykes (Fig. 1). These brown-weathering, north- to northeast- trending dykes, up to 45 m wide, are characterized by coarse clinopyroxene (25%), orthopyroxene (20%), and olivine (5%) in a matrix of calcic plagioclase (45%) and accessory Fe–Ti oxides, biotite, and apatite. They are generally fresh with minor uralitic

to 45 m wide, are characterized by coarse clinopyroxene (25%), orthopyroxene (20%), and olivine (5%) in a matrix of calcic plagioclase (45%) and accessory Fe–Ti oxides, biotite, and apatite. a Klotz dykes trend west-northwest, but do not carry a consistent magnetization direction. Finally, 199 8±2M aM i n t o dykes of west-northwest to northwest trend, identical in age to the 1998 M a±2M aP u r t u n i qophiolite of the Cape Smith Belt, have a paleopole at 38°N, 174°E. The similarity of paleopoles for the ca. 2.23–2.21 Ga Maguire dykes of the Minto block, Senneterre dykes of the southern Superior, and Nipissing sills of the Southern Province demonstrates that these regions were in their present relative latitudes and orientations at that time. . Following the major tectonic activity, metamorphism, and plutonism at ca. 2.7 Ga, the Minto block cooled to record ca. 2.5 Ga K–Ar mica dates. It was transected by several swarms of diabase dykes (Fig. 1), some of which are likely linked to Paleoproterozoic rifting events (ca. 2.2–2.0 Ga) at the margins of the Superior Province. Only minor deforma - tion and retrogression of the Superior craton is associated with subsequent (ca. 1.8 Ga) compressional orogeny in the New Quebec and Ungava orogens. In this study, the Ptarmigan, Maguire, Klotz, and Minto dyke swarms (Fig. 1) are defined on the basis of their U–Pb geochronology, paleomagnetism, petrographic characteris- tics, and trend. The extent of Ptarmigan, Maguire, and Minto swarms is poorly defined because the dykes are not readily traceable on aeromagnetic maps. Dykes of the Klotz swarm are also not evident on aeromagnetic maps, but can be easily traced on aerial photographs. The 2505 Ma Ptarmigan swarm consists of only a few dykes (Fig. 1). These brown-weathering, north- to northeast- trending dykes, up to 45 m wide, are characterized by coarse clinopyroxene (25%), orthopyroxene (20%), and olivine (5%) in a matrix of calcic plagioclase (45%) and accessory Fe–Ti oxides, biotite, and apatite. These coarse-grained, ophitic dykes consist of euhedral plagioclase lathes (50%) in a matrix of subhedral to anhedral pyroxene, including zoned titanaugite and minor orthopyroxene. alytical techniques Samples for U–Pb geochronology were obtained from the coarse interiors of four of the thickest dykes, one in each of the Ptarmigan, Maguire, Minto, and Klotz swarms (Fig. 1, 2). Zircon and (or) baddeleyite were separated from 5–25 kg samples using conventional crushing, grinding, wet shaking table, heavy liquids, and magnetic separator methods. Indi - vidual fractions for analysis were selected on the basis of grain size and morphology. Analyses at the Geochronology Laboratory of the Geological Survey of Canada (Ottawa) used methods described by Mortensen (1993) and Buchan et al. (1993). All zircon fractions analysed were air abraded prior to dissolution. Baddeleyite grains were not abraded. The similarity of paleopoles for the ca. 2.23–2.21 Ga Maguire dykes of the Minto block, Senneterre dykes of the southern Superior, and Nipissing sills of the Southern Province demonstrates that these regions were in their present relative latitudes and orientations at that time. The Maguire, Senneterre, and Klotz dykes form a roughly radiating pattern and may represent one quadrant of a giant radiating dyke swarm centred southeast of Ungava Bay, whose focus marks the location of a mantle plume responsible for ca. 2.22 Ga breakup along the eastern margin of the Superior Province. n 1997223. 2Corresponding author (e-mail: kbuchan@NRCan.gc.ca). 1 I:\cjes\cjes35\cjes-09\E98-054.vp Tuesday, December 22, 1998 10:49:14 Color profile: Disabled Composite Default screen Numerous diabase dyke swarms, mostly of Proterozoic age, intrude the Superior Province of the Canadian Shield and are thought to record periodic extensional magmatism linked to events at the margins of the craton. Recent collabo - rative studies of paleomagnetism and U–Pb geochronology of dyke swarms of the southern Superior Province have yielded precise ages for Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles and have resulted in a major revision of the Paleoproterozoic apparent polar wander path for this area (Buchan et al. 1993, 1994, 1996). Fragmental rocks of the lower unit of the Carmacks Group include coarse olivine, pyroxene, and feldspar porphyritic vol- canoclastic and volcanoglomeratic rocks, laminated felsic and mafic tuff, shale, and mudstone. Subordinate flows of andesite and basaltic andesite are interbedded with the fragmental rocks. Isolated rhyodacite flows are locally present at the base and the top of the unit. Alteration, including saussuritization, bleaching, and sericite and hematite alteration, is common. Quartz chalcedony forms agates, lines and fills cavities, coats individual clasts, and fills crosscutting fractures. The thickest, coarsest accumulations of fragmental volcanic rocks define a number of volcanic complexes that are commonly cored by small (1 km 2) granitic to syenitic intrusions. The areally extensive flat-lying flows of the upper flood- basalt unit overlie the fragmental unit along a small (<10°) angular unconformity. Site mean directions and reversal and fold tests The mean directions for each site are listed in Table 1. The formational averages are listed in Table 2. The site mean di- rections plotted in Fig. 7 show that each locality has a well-de- fined mean direction, but that they are dispersed after correction for bedding. On the other hand, in present coordi- nates, they are highly clustered. The degree of unfolding which provides the tightest concentration is at 1 ± 5% (Watson and Enkin 1993), indicating a highly significant negative fold test. The beds were first deformed and then remagnetized. However, the Alaska Highway (country rock and high-tem- perature components within the dyke contact zones) and the Takhini Hotspring sites are all normally magnetized, whereas those from Sid’s Quarry contain a reverse polarity, indicating that they were not remagnetized at exactly the same time. With respect to present horizontal, the angular difference between the two polarity groups is 3.2± 7.1° away from antipodal (95% confidence interval, method of Debiche and Watson 1995), indicating that the sites were remagnetized over a period with no significant apparent polar wander, but long enough (>10 ka) to average out secular variation. Mid-Cretaceous volcanic rocks con- sist of andesitic feldspar porphyry flows and tuffs of the Mount Nansen Group. Felsic volcanic rocks deposited across south- central Yukon between 84 and 78 Ma, including pyroclastic flows and flow-banded rhyolite, are included in the Windy–Table Suite (Mihalynuk et al. 1992; Hart 1995). Specimens were measured in the laboratory using a robotized Schonstedt DSM1 fluxgate magnetometer or a Geofyzika JR5A spinner magnetometer. Fragmental rocks of the lower unit of the Carmacks Group include coarse olivine, pyroxene, and feldspar porphyritic vol- canoclastic and volcanoglomeratic rocks, laminated felsic and mafic tuff, shale, and mudstone. Subordinate flows of andesite and basaltic andesite are interbedded with the fragmental rocks. Isolated rhyodacite flows are locally present at the base and the top of the unit. Alteration, including saussuritization, bleaching, and sericite and hematite alteration, is common. Quartz chalcedony forms agates, lines and fills cavities, coats individual clasts, and fills crosscutting fractures. The thickest, coarsest accumulations of fragmental volcanic rocks define a number of volcanic complexes that are commonly cored by small (1 km 2) granitic to syenitic intrusions. The areally extensive flat-lying flows of the upper flood- basalt unit overlie the fragmental unit along a small (<10°) angular unconformity. All the ice sheets originated from distant sources located to the south- east of Banks Island on the Canadian mainland. The purpose of this study was to apply paleomagnetism as a tool to define better the chronology of events, and to relate them to the global polarity time scale and the oceanic isotope record. Vincent (1983, 1984, 1989, 1990, 1992) reconstructed a sequence of nonglacial and glacial events (Table 1). At the base, he identified a nonglacial interval recorded by the Worth Point Formation. Glaciation began with the extensive continental Banks Glacia- tion. Evidence shows that the Sahli granite magnetization was acquired during a metamorphic event which probably peaked in the interval 1840–1800 Ma. The reset nature of the Sahli granite data is partly supported by a negative contact test from a cross-cutting maﬁc dyke. The Paleogene Ethiopian volcanic province [12] was not investigated using the above mentioned tech- niques until a French±Ethiopian cooperative project was launched in 1993. The province is now split by continental break-up around the Afar depres- sion, with the major part forming the NW Ethiopian plateau (partly dismantled to the N in Eritrea), and minor parts on the east side of the main Ethiopian rift (Somalia plate) and on the Arabian plate in Yemen (Fig. 1). The southern Ethiopian Eocene volcanic province, which may constitute a separate province both in time and space [13], is not included in the present discussion. Geological setting and sampling Late Cretaceous±early Paleocene arc-related complexes are exposed mainly in the NNE±SSW trending Median Range and the East Ranges tectonic zones of Kamchatka. The Median Range complex is thrust over the West zone of Kamchatka along the large gently dipping Lesnov thrust of north±west vergence. logous to those of terrigenous ¯ysch of the Ukelayat zone of the Koryak High- lands; this ¯ysch contains Campanian±Maastrichtian radiolaria and Paleocene±early Eocene foraminifera [4,12]. Furthermore, in the West zone of Kamchatka, lithological counterparts of the Lesnov Series greatly differ from overlying late Paleocene coal-bearing sediments of continental provenance [13]. Self reversing behaviour is found in some volcanic rocks of dacitic and andesitic com- positions [31±33]. Such rocks can contain two ferro- magnetic minerals, one of which is in the ilmenite± hematite series (Fe 2/NULyTiyO3) with 0:45 y 0:65. Curie temperatures corresponding to these composi- tions lie between 280 and 50ëC, which are the un- blocking temperatures of most self-reversed TRMs found in nature. Here, the ITC persists to at least 400ëC. Two alternative explanations for the ITC are: (1) the rock contains two ferromagnetic minerals that grew at different times (e.g., primary crystallization followed by hydrothermal alteration), one during a period of normal polarity and the other when the Earth's ®eld was reversed; or (2) site 01 was heated during a period of reversed polarity and grains with high bulk coercivities were preferentially thermally remagnetized during the heating

Discussion and conclusions The main conclusion evinced from this palaeo- magnetic study is that the Upper Triassic to Middle Jurassic sediments are overprinted. Because the pole to bedding of the Lower Cretaceous andesites lies in the same swath as the older sediments (Fig. 1), we assume that a single deformation event is respon- sible for the folding of all the rocks; thus the age of folding (and C1 remanence acquisition) is prob- ably post-Early Cretaceous. Conclusions A paleomagnetic study of the Early Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation, exposed in the northern reaches of the Argentine Precordillera has yielded the first reliable Early Paleozoic paleomagnetic pole for this terrane. A pre-tectonic, probably primary remanence, car- ried by hematite or magnetite, was isolated from ten sampling sites. The studied locality, the northeastern- most yet sampled from Early Paleozoic rocks of the Argentine Precordillera, apparently escaped the widespread Early Permian remagnetization that af- fected many other units of this age in this region. The paleomagnetic pole is not consistent with the 550±500 Ma path from the already assembled Gond- wana. Instead, if the Precordillera is located against the southeastern margin of Laurentia it becomes perfectly consistent with coeval poles from Lauren- tia. The Ligurian units represent the accretionary wedge re- sulting from the subduction of the Ligurian ocean below the Corsica±Sardinia block, and were thrust during the Neogene to the northeast onto the Tus- can±Umbria carbonate successions of the Adria pas- .sive continental margin Fig. 1 . Thrusting was ac- companied by clastic sedimentation in northeast- wxward-migrating foredeeps 6 . The Tuscan±Umbria units were in turn thrust onto the `autochthonous' metamorphic complex now exposed in the Apuane wxAlps 7 . Clastics referred to in the literature as Epiligurian units were also deposited in relatively undeformed basins located on top of the advancing Ligurian thrust sheets. The Epiligurian units, which we sampled at 26 .sites Fig. 1 , consist of Middle Eocene to Pliocene clastic sediments characterized by strong lateral vari- ations in lithology and thickness. These sediments were mainly deposited in deep-water marine envi- ronments where tectonic activity often generated slumpings and olistostromes on unstable slopes. The Ligurian units represent the accretionary wedge re- sulting from the subduction of the Ligurian ocean below the Corsica±Sardinia block, and were thrust during the Neogene to the northeast onto the Tus- can±Umbria carbonate successions of the Adria pas- .sive continental margin Fig. 1 . Clastics referred to in the literature as Epiligurian units were also deposited in relatively undeformed basins located on top of the advancing Ligurian thrust sheets. This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed

Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Demagnetization experiments revealed two distinct remanence components in the Ordovician carbonate rocks: (1) a dual polarity Permian-Triassic magnetization carried by magnetite that was acquired after Paleozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall, mean directions for all three magnetizations roughly coincide with corresponding refer- ence directions for Nevada. ozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall, mean directions for all three magnetizations roughly coincide with corresponding refer- ence directions for Nevada. The largest decli- nation discordance of 16° ± 7° (clockwise) comes from comparison of the Permian- Triassic magnetite magnetization to the Late Permian reference direction for Nevada. Thus, although structural and geothermal data, including zircon fission-track ages, indi- cate that northern Bare Mountain was tilted 20°–40° northeastward about a horizontal axis during early Tertiary time, we find no ev- idence for large-scale (i.e., >30°) vertical-axis rotation. Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise rotations are also observed in the Black Moun- tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat- eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton- wood Mountain

resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions from most of the middle Miocene volcanic rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992; Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al., 1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996). Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in- dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993). Structural and sedimentological evidence for large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Snow (1992; 1994), for example, envisioned the Pan- ama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts exposed at Bare Mountain as rotated segments of an Early Per- mian, pre-Sonoma thrust system that is also ex- posed in the Cottonwood Range in northern Death Valley. Reconstruction of the thrust system predicts large-scale translation along a Cenozoic regional detachment and a 90° clockwise vertic

In this model, the Amargosa Desert fault system, which includes the Bare Mountain fault, has presumably accumulated more than 30 km of dextral displacement since the mid-Miocene with minimal vertical-axis rota- tion of the Bare Mountain block. This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed in nearby ranges of the Yucca Mountain region, as well as previously published paleomagnetic results from other ranges in Nevada and Utah. Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise rotations are also observed in the Black Moun- tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat- eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton- wood Mountain

resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions from most of the middle Miocene volcanic rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992; Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al., 1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996). Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in- dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993). Structural and sedimentological evidence for large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Snow (1992; 1994), for example, envisioned the Pan- ama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts exposed at Bare Mountain as rotated segments of an Early Per- mian, pre-Sonoma thrust system that is also ex- posed in the Cottonwood Range in northern Death Valley. Reconstruction of the thrust system predicts large-scale translation along a Cenozoic regional detachment and a 90° clockwise vertic

In this model, the Amargosa Desert fault system, which includes the Bare Mountain fault, has presumably accumulated more than 30 km of dextral displacement since the mid-Miocene with minimal vertical-axis rota- tion of the Bare Mountain block. This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed in nearby ranges of the Yucca Mountain region, as well as previously published paleomagnetic results from other ranges in Nevada and Utah. In southern California, characteristic magnetizations for remnants of the Coast Range ophiolite (Stanley Mountain, Point Sal, Cuesta Ridge, Llanada) have been consistently interpreted as having been acquired at low palcolatitudes [Luyendyk and Hornafius, 1982; McWilliams and Howell, 1982; Beebe and Luyendyk, 1983], but field stability tests are also lacking, and only normal polarity is indicated at each locality; therefore these results are also consistent with subsequent remagnetization. Recent studies of ophiolitic rocks at Stanley Mountain [Hagstrum, !992; Hagstrum and Murchey, 1996] and on the Vizcaino Peninsula in Baja California [Hagstrum et al., 1993] indicate definitively that these rocks have been magnetically overprinted. een acquired at low palcolatitudes [Luyendyk and Hornafius, 1982; McWilliams and Howell, 1982; Beebe and Luyendyk, 1983], but field stability tests are also lacking, and only normal polarity is indicated at each locality; therefore these results are also consistent with subsequent remagnetization. Recent studies of ophiolitic rocks at Stanley Mountain [Hagstrum, !992; Hagstrum and Murchey, 1996] and on the Vizcaino Peninsula in Baja California [Hagstrum et al., 1993] indicate definitively that these rocks have been magnetically overprinted. We present a magnetostratigraphic study of three pelagic limestone sections (Gamsstein, Mendlingbach and Mayerling) from the eastern part of the Northern Calcareous Alps. Together these sections, which contain a rich conodont fauna, yield a sedimentary record encompassing the uppermost Anisian, the Ladinian and the Lower Carnian. Thermal demagnetization and isothermal remanent magnetization experiments indicate that the magnetization is essentially carried by a mineral of the magnetite family. The high unblocking temperature components isolated from the three sections provide clear magnetic polarity zonations. Correlations between these results, based on the biostratigraphic data and tephrochronology, allow the construction of a composite magnetic polarity sequence from the Illyrian substage (Upper Anisian) to the Julian 2 zone (Lower Carnian). According to Nicora and Brack [1995], these intervals fit closely in age ith the three Reifling basin layers. Geological Setting, Lithology and Sampling The studied sections are located in the eastern part of the Northern Calcareous Alps, within the so-called Bajuvaricum mega-unit. The discordance between the two groups is striking, given that recent U-Pb dating of rocks from the Belt Supergroup demonstrates that most of the rocks from which the two groups of poles are derived are approximately coeval [Aleinikoff et al., 1996]. All magnetic measurements and demagnetizations were performed in the magnetically shielded room of the Paleomagnetic Laboratory at the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP) / Université de Paris 7 and also in the Magnetism Laboratory of Saint Maur (IPGP). Remanent magnetizations were measured with a Three-component CTF inc. cryogenic magnetometer. Apparent ages for each temperature step were calculated using the decay constants recommended by Steiger and Jiiger [ 1977]. A common occurrence of hematite (in some specimens making 40 to 50% of all the grains) is as aligned inclusions in detrital mica and chlorite (Figure 5). Some inclusions are lensoidal in shape, others are planar. Inclusions are often truncated at grain boundaries and in some cases they are deformed through compaction. There is almost no evidence of hematite dissolution and no cases of hematite forming around the mica grains except for small stains of hematite pigment in the most oxidized grains. These grains are completely enclosed in calcite cement, and, in some instances, cement crosscuts inclusions. Paleomagnetic data for the Newark Supergroup, on which the hypothesis of small to negligible APW is based, include the mid to upper Camian Stockton and Lockatong formations, the lower to upper Norian Passaic Formation, and overlying Hettangian basalts and sedimentary rocks (an interval from -228 to 205 Ma). Other paleomagnetic data, however, have been interpreted to indicate that Late Triassic APW of North America is significant. Kodama et al. [1994] showed evidence of Late Triassic APW from Mesozoic rocks of noaheast

for strata of unquestionably different age. A few million years would not affect previous estimates of large CP rotation if Late Triassic APW was indeed negligible, but the age difference between cratonic and CP poles is sufficient to bias a rotation estimate if APW was rapid. The new pole for the upper Carnian Bluewater Creek Formation reported here provides a datum of crucial importance to (1) test the hypothesis of a Late Triassic stand still in the North American APW path and (2) improve estimates of CP rotation based on Triassic results. This manuscript focuses on the first issue; regardless of the magnitude of CP rotation, paleopoles from rocks on and off the plateau should record similar amounts of APW. From the determination of two new pole positions and teevaluation of previously published data, we suggest that APW was neither small nor slow during the Late Triassic. This is important not only for understanding the kinematics of deformation along the western margin of North America but also in determining the motion of the North American craton during the Mesozoic. Samples were oriented using both magnetic compass and solar compass. No significant deviations were noted between these orientation methods. An additional 14 samples were taken from slumped blocks at one particular level of the Vilavila Formation. The preservation of recognizable bedding in these slump blocks allowed us to use these samples in a modified conglomerate test. Following sample preparation, all specimens were stored and analyzed in a magnetically shielded room with background field intensity < 200 nT. NRM was measured with a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer (2G model 755R). Thermal demagne- tizations at 14 to 18 steps up to 680øC were accomplished using furnaces with magnetic field intensity less than 10 nT in the sample region. Results of thermal demagnetization were analyzed by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and site-mean directions were determined using the statistical methods of Fisher [1953]. Analyses of coercivity spectra of 11 representative samples were performed using the methods of Dunlop [1972] and Lowrie [1990]. Factors limiting the precision with which the characteristic directions can be used to infer age of remagnetization and tec- tonic disturbance subsequent to remagnetization include the following: (1) The major variation in bedding attitudes within the Pongo sampling area allows the percent of folding at remagnetization to be fairly tightly constrained to 20% fold- ing (Figure 7). However, the major sampled stratigraphic sequence at Villamontes is nearly homoclinal and that section has only a modest contrast of bedding attitude with other sam- pling localities in that region. Accordingly, assignment of percent folding at the time of remagnetization of Paleozoic strata at Villamontes lacks precision (Figure 8). (2) The mag- nitude of APW as viewed from South America is modest during Mesozoic and Cenozoic time [Irving and Irving, 1982; Besse and Courtillot, 1991]. Therefore only very low resolution is possible when inferring ages of magnetization by matching

robably not preserved in sedimentary strata in this region. Future attempts to obtain primary paleomagnetic directions from Paleozoic rocks of the Andes should focus on less deformed regions, per- haps in the forebulge region of the active foreland basin. Finally, the documentation of this remagnetization reaffirms the critical importance of multiple field tests of paleomagnetic stability when applying paleomagnetic methods to rocks in orogenic zones. Factors limiting the precision with which the characteristic directions can be used to infer age of remagnetization and tec- tonic disturbance subsequent to remagnetization include the following: (1) The major variation in bedding attitudes within the Pongo sampling area allows the percent of folding at remagnetization to be fairly tightly constrained to 20% fold- ing (Figure 7). Late Cretaceous-Paleogene paleomagnetic pole for Sikhote Alin Reliable reversed polarity directions appear from the high- and middle-temperature remanent magnetization components at 25 sites in the Bo- gopol and Sijanov groups. The K-Ar results as- sign ages of 51 and 53 Ma to the former group, and 66 Ma to the latter group. Reversed polarity is dominant during the period between 66 Ma and 51 Ma [22]. A primary origin for their rema- nent magnetization was ascertained by the pre- dominance of the reversed polarity, the stable behavior under thermal demagnetization and a closer grouping of the paleomagnetic directions after tilt correction. A Late Cretaceous-early Paleogene pole was evaluated on the basis of data set of both the Sijanov and the Bogopol groups. Since formation ages for the Bogopol and Sijanov groups cover a fairly long duration, between 51 Ma and 66 Ma, the secular variation is almost certainly averaged out. This paper reports the paleomagnetic and geochronological analysis of a suite of samples from a basaltic fault-related scarp of Pliocene age in the central part of the Afar depression (Ethiopia). Paleomagnetic work uncovers a clear characteristic remanent magnetization carried by (titano-) magnetites, with high unblocking temperatures, close to the Curie temperature of pure magnetite. The characteristic direction, based on 27 non transitional flows, is D=8.1 o, I= 10.1 o (5=4.1 o). This is consistent with earlier determinations of the clockwise tectonic rotation, due to rift propagation and overlap, of the block to which the section belongs. Magnetic stratigraphy consists of a succession from bottom to top of 16 reversed, 7 normal, and 4 reversed flows. [1993] and used in the GPTS. 1. Introduction The Afar triangle lies at the triple junction of the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Ethiopian rifts. The floor of the triangular depression is mostly covered by young lava, most prominently by the widespread so-called stratoid basalts [Varet, 1975]. These basalts were severely faulted as the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea rifts propagated toward each other [Courtillot, 1980, 1982] and now form an active overlap [Tapponnier et al., 1990; Manighetti, 1993; Manighetti et al., 1997]. Acquisition of paleomagnetic and geochronologic data has been a key to understanding the tectonics of the area. Courtillot et al. [1984] suggested that much of the trap-like stratoid series had been emplaced relatively fast between 1.3 and 2.2 Ma and demonstrated important block rotations of some 10 ø to 15 ø. Mid-Cretaceous volcanic rocks con- sist of andesitic feldspar porphyry flows and tuffs of the Mount Nansen Group. Felsic volcanic rocks deposited across south- central Yukon between 84 and 78 Ma, including pyroclastic flows and flow-banded rhyolite, are included in the Windy–Table Suite (Mihalynuk et al. 1992; Hart 1995). The solar and magnetic bearings agreed within 2° except where the rocks had been hit by lightning and were, as a consequence, strongly magnetic. Solar bearings were used for these rocks. Specimens were measured in the laboratory using a robotized Schonstedt DSM1 fluxgate magnetometer or a Geofyzika JR5A spinner magnetometer. Three sites (W61–W63) were collected from isolated outcrops along the Klondike Highway north of Carmacks. The cores from the Carmacks Agate Quarry (site W61) are relatively unaltered, finely crystalline basalt with 0.2–5 cm quartz-filled amygdules. It appears, therefore, that, like the Mandanna Member, the Nordenskiöld Formation at this locality was totally overprinted, after tilting, at the time of extrusion of the Carmacks Group. The interpretation for the Cinnamon Bun Row locality re- manence is less straightforward. The mean direction before tectonic correction is nearly vertical, which implies magneti- zation at the north pole. But after tectonic correction, the di- rection is shallow even compared with the Carmacks remanence. There are at least three ways this result can be interpreted: (i) the remanence could be primary, but it is shal- low compared with other Jurassic paleomagnetic data obtained in the southern Intermontane Belt (e.g., Monger and Irving 1980); (ii) the remanence could be a predeformational Creta- ceous overprint, implying an approximately 60° clockwise vertical axis rotation; and (iii) the remanence could be a post- deformational Cretaceous overprint followed by a further tilt of 20° down towards 347°NNW. Tilts of this magnitude have been observed in the Carmacks Formation elsewhere and so it is not unreasonable to invoke a late tilt. This explains the dis- crepancy between the locality mean direction of Cinnamon Bun Row (tilted after being overprinted during extrusion of the Carmacks Group) and that of Atlin Lake (not tilted after over- printing), and we favour this interpretation. The sites are scat- tered over the entire area of SE Tinos (Fig. 2A). Six field-drilled cores were collected from each site, ori- ented in the field by both sun compass and a Brunton compass. Remnant magnetization of all samples was measured using a three-axis 2-G super conducting magnetometer with integrated alternating field (AF) coils, at the Geophysical Institute of Israel, Holon (Israel). Summary and conclusions Our study was aimed to constrain the mode of post-12 Ma crustal extension in the Cyclades area, particularly in the vicinity of the islands of Tinos and Mykonos. K-Ar analyses yielded ages of 11.5 f0.4 Ma indicating that these dikes wit- nessed a substantial part of the extensional history of the central Aegean region. We assume that the dacitic dikes intruded vertical (as they are today) and that no tilt correction is required. This is supported by the fact that no inclination anomaly is revealed when the palaeomagnetic data is compared with a tilt-corrected pole position from Kimi (Evia). The absence of tilting implies that post-12 Ma crustal thinning in the area of Tinos island was minor. On Mykonos. a low-angle normal fault dipping 30” to the NE juxtaposes a series of Oligo-Miocene molasse sediments above a IO- 12-Ma granite. Published palaeomagnetic data revealed a considerable amount of inclination flattening and 22” clockwise rotation of the footwall granite. We show that tilting predated vertical-axis rotation, and that the (now) low-angle normal fault originated steeper, dipping ca. 54”. Planar-rotational fault geometry indicates extension of ca. 60%. In spite of the significant variations in the magnitude of post-12 Ma upper crustal extension across the Tinos-Mykonos transect, crustal thickness below the entire area changes only slightly. The widespread Middle Miocene granitic magmatism in the Cyclades suggests that flow in the lower crust may have had a dominant role in maintaining the smooth Moho. Assuming that the western Cyclades constitute a set of NW-striking crustal blocks, it is estimated that vertical-axis rotations increased the N-S dimension of the area by ca. 3 I % (e.g. 25 km). It contains several petrologic phases ranging from gabbro to tonalite. It is massive and unmetamorphosed, the youngest major pluton in the collage, and it was emplaced at 1838 Ma into low-grade metamorphic rocks. Paleomagnetic analyses using alternating field and thermal step demagnetization methods were run on 229 specimens from 24 sites in and adjacent to the pluton. Its characteristic remanent magnetization direction (ChRM) is shown from thermal demagnetization and saturation isothermal remanence analyses to reside mostly in single domain to multidomain magnetite, commonly with high unblocking temperatures near the 585°C Curie temperature, but sometimes in pyrrhotite. Vertical late-phase diabase and felsic dike sites intersect about at right angles, indicating that the pluton has not been tilted since emplacement. It provides, along with the Reynard Lake pluton's pole, an apparent polar wander path segment for the Amisk collage. This path is compared with coeval segments from the Superior craton, Hanson Lake block and Lynn Lake-La Ronge domain. Together the segments display the classical paleomagnetic signature for a collisional orogen with the crustal allochthons of the southeastern THO accreting to the Superior craton at -1830 Ma. 1. From stratigraphic data Kolata and Nelson (1991) estimate uplift at between 2.4 and 4.6 km. Similarly, Leach et al. (1994) set uplift at between 2.1 and 3.7 km using conodont alteration index val- ues. Arguing that some time must be left for erosion of the uplift prior to overlying Late Cretaceous sedi- mentation, Kolata and Nelson (1991, fig. 1) suggest an end to uplift in mid-Jurassic time. This uplift must be assumed to have been in response to large intra- plate tectonic forces and to have caused a major pe- riod of reactivation on the fluorspar district faults. The speculation is, therefore, that the Rosiclare event coincides with the Mesozoic uplift event with concomitant fault reactivation and northeasterly fluid flow in the Reelfoot-Wabash rift zone. An obvious speculation is that hot brines moving northeasterly from deep in the Reelfoot rift on Pas- cola arch uplift (Goldhaber et al., 1992b; Leach et al., 1994) may have met and mixed with lower tem- perature brines at the juncture with the crosscutting Ste. The rank of the Pennsylvanian coal beds in the area indicates only 1,300 m of burial (Schwalb, 1982) and the dominant fluid inclusion temperatures of 140 ø to 153øC also limit postemplacement heating to less than about 100øC. ociated with any known igneous intrusions. Mississippian limestones from some 200 km to the northeast near Louisville, which are stratigraphi- cally equivalent to the host rocks, retain an A charac- teristic RM component. SYMONS Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada N9B 3P44 Abstract The Illinois-Kentucky fluorspar district has yielded most of the United States fluorite pro- duction. The fluorspar ore occurs as epigenetic replacement deposits in Mississippian lime- stone and as vein deposits. Palcomagnetic analysis was done on 324 specimens from 33 sites in fluorspar ore and in host limestones and cap-rock sandstones both adjacent to and remote from ore using alternating field and thermal step demagnetization. Saturation isothermal remanence methods were used to identify magnetization carriers in typical specimens and mineral crystals. An A characteristic remanent magnetization (RM) component was found outside the district in stratigraphically equivalent limestones that record a Pennsylvanian Kiaman remagnetization, and a C characteristic RM was found in surface weathered speci- mens that records the Recent earth's magnetic field. At 28 sites in ore and nearby host rocks a B characteristic RM was found that gives a Late Jurassic pole position of 152.4 ø E, 78.0 ø N (dp = 3.0 ø, dm = 4.4ø). Late Jurassic genesis for the fluorspar fits withi

g of subsur- face fluids of uncertain age (e.g., Richardson and Pinckney, 1984). The object of this study was to use palcomagnetic methods to date the ore and, thereby, to constrain geologic models for genesis of the fluor- spar ore. Geology The Illinois-Kentucky fluorspar district covers an area of about 2,500 km 2 straddling the southern Illi- nois-western Kentucky boundary (Fig. 1). Baxter et al. (1989) have recently summarized the extensive geologic literature of the district. The Precambrian basement of the Illinois-Ken- tucky fluorspar district is overlain by Cambrian to Pennsylvanian sedimentary rocks that host two end- member types of epigenetic fluorspar deposits-- manto or bedding replacement deposits that grade into fissure-filling vein deposits (Grogan and Brad- bury, 1968). Genevieve Lime- stone beds beneath the Rosiclare Sandstone Member, and Bethel ore in limestones of the uppermost beds of the Downeys Bluff Member of the Renault Forma- tion beneath the Bethel Sandstone Member (Baxter et al., 1992). The mantos range up to 3 km in length, 60 m in width, and 6 m in thickness; they occur next to major northeast-trending faults beneath cap-rock sandstones. The vein deposits are predominantly in the northeast-trending faults and mainly within the walls of the middle Mississippian strata. However, trace amounts of fluorite are found in faults cutting lower Pennsylvanian rocks. The vein deposits range up to about 250 m vertically and horizontally and up to 14 m in width. Its geology is known primarily from drilling for niobium, apatite, and limestone deposits (Parsons 1961; Sage et al. 1982; Sage 1983). Three to six oriented cores were drilled from each of these meager, moss- covered outcrops, giving nine sites in total (Fig. 2). Measurements were made with an automated Canadian Thin Films cryogenic magnetometer, a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 alternating-field (AF) demagnetizer and direct-current (DC) magnetizer, and a Schonstedt TSD- 1 thermal demagnetizer. It intrudes granulite-rank Archean gneisses in the Kapuskasing Structural Zone of the Wawa Subprovince in the Superior Province of the Canadian Shield. It adjoins the Ivanhoe Lake fault zone, which forms the boundary with the Abitibi Subprovince and is the probable locus of maximum motion between the subprovinces. Specimens from 18 sites in the complex were analyzed paleomagnetically by alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and by saturation isothermal remanence tests. They have been cut by the Early Proterozoic Hearst diabase dikes, which trend north-south and dip nearly vertically (Emst and Halls 1984). The complex is nearly circular, with a diameter of about 5.5 km. It comprises dominantly massive, coarse-grained leucocratic nepheline syenite that forms both the core and the periphery. In between are arcuate bands and partial rings of foliated malignite - ijolite that dip at 40° - 65 towards the centre. Within these bands on the north side is a small zone of calcic carbonatite. On the west side of these bands is an inte- rior zone of iiolite breccia, with abundant magnetite, and on the north side is an exterior zone of ijolite breccia called the Portage Lake Complex. The syenite and mafic alkalic rocks are cut in turn by carbonatite veins with pyrochlore that carry the niobium values, by the apatite - magnetite veins, and finally by occasional lamprophyre dikes that are not exposed. The contacts of the complex are apparently vertical, and the adjacent wall rocks are fenitized. There is no petrologic evi- dence of postintrusive metamorphism of the complex. Minor late north-northeast-trending faults with displace- ments of a few tens of metres have been interpreted from the ground magnetometer surveys

carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Yet another possibility is that the pole reflects a postintrusive metamorphic event. This seems untenable for several reasons. First, the rocks show no evidence of postintrusive metamor- phism (Sage 1983). Second, excluding perhaps the nearly con- temporaneous Nemegosenda Complex, there are no known younger intrusions in the area. Third, the step-demagnetization I data show no evidence of an underlying older remanence com- ponent. Fourth, the APWP is not known to pass through the Lackner Lake position at any subsequent time (Irving 1979). Thus the best and preferred explanation is that the Lackner pole is concordant and reflects a primary untilted remanence direction. Recently, Halls and Pesonen (1982) and Palmer and Davis (1987) evalu- ated the paleomagnetic and radiometric data base for the Logan Loop, and the Lackner pole falls at about 1108 f 10 Ma on it (Fig. 7). This paleomagnetic age agrees well with the K- Ar age of 1086 f 60 Ma and the pooled Rb - Sr isochron age of 1092 f 21 Ma. It is, however, a normal pole in a reversed- polarity part of the APWP. The simplest explanation is that the complex records a brief normal-polarity interval in a dorni- nantly reversed portion of the path. Another explanation could be that the complex is actually about 1090 Ma old, in which case its original pole position would be close to MPl (Fig. 7). If true, then the complex would have to have been tilted about 30°W about a horizontal north-northeast axis to give its present pole. Yet another possibility is that the pole reflects a postintrusive metamorphic event. This seems untenable for several reasons. First, the rocks show no evidence of postintrusive metamor- phism (Sage 1983). Second, excluding perhaps the nearly con- temporaneous Nemegosenda Complex, there are no known younger intrusions in the area. Third, the step-demagnetization I data show no evidence of an underlying older remanence com- ponent. Fourth, the APWP is not known to pass through the Lackner Lake position at any subsequent time (Irving 1979). Thus the best and preferred explanation is that the Lackner pole is concordant and reflects a primary untilted remanence direction. ferous limestone and chert clasts from the Cache Creek Terrane into Middle to Late Jurassic conglomerates of the Bowser Basin. Similarly, the Early Jurassic Inkdin Formation of the Cache Creek Terrane contains detritus believed to be derived from the Quesnellia terrane (Monger et al. 1991). Thus, by Middle Jurassic, the Stikinia, Quesnellia, and Cache Greek terranes were at least loosely amalgamated and located next to the craton. Previous paleomagnetic studies suggest that the terranes underlying the Insular Belt (Fig. 2) may have collided with those of the Intermontane Belt by mid-Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous time to create a fairly coherent assemblage located some 1000-2880 km south of its present position (Irving and Wynne 1991 ; Irving et al. 1996), with the Coast Plutonic Complex marking the intervening suture (Monger et al. 1982). Subsequently, this assemblage of terranes moved north-northwesterly in panels on dominantly dextral faults beside the North American craton, reaching their present position in the Late Eocene ( - 45 Ma) (Irving et ad. 1996). Paleomagnetic data for Eocene (52 -44 Ma) rocks throughout the Canadian Cordillera, except for the Queen Charlotte Islands (Irving and Wynne 1991), show that the Cordilleran terranes have not moved signif

al and glaciolacustrine alluvium that obscures its eastern margin (Hart and Radloff 1990). Aeromagnetic surveys indi- cate its eastern contact dips steeply, and drilling indicates a steep to locally overhanging contact on the west and an out- ward shallow-dipping contact on its north and south sides (Morrison 1981; Hart and Pelletier 1989). Contact attitudes indicate that the pluton has not been tilted, assuming vertical emplacement. Pendants of host rock are numerous dong the northern, western, and southern margins, but are not observed along the eastern margin because of lower erosional levels and the presence of the overburden. Based on thin-section analyses and field observations for all paleomagnetic sites and elsewhere, the rock types include diorite, quartz diorite, quartz monzo- diorite, tonalite, and granodiorite. Most have medium- to coarse-grained plagioclase in a fine- to medium-grained matrix of quartz and mafic minerals (Hart and Radloff 1990). The major minerals are plagioclase, quartz, hornblende, and biotite. Minor and accessory minerals include magnetite, potassium feldspar, titanite, and apatite. Larger hornblende crystals typically have clinopyroxene cores. The anorthite content of plagioclase ranges from Anl9 to An34 (average Anz5), and some albite may be present. Visible potassium feldspar crystals are rare, but perthite is common. The pluton is variably altered, as the presence of chlorite, epidote, and carbonate suggests. Zones of hydrothermal alteration in the northern part of the pluton are probably related to adjacent copper -gold skarn deposits in that region (Morrison 198 1 ; Hart and Pelletier 1989 ; Hart and Radloff 1990; Hart 1995). It is in fault contact on the east with the Cache Creek Terrane, but the origind nature of its western contact has been masked by Cretaceous and Tertiary plutonism and metamorphism of the Coast Plutonic Complex. The upper Paleozoic and Triassic rocks of Stikinia are thought to reflect an island-arc setting, with its 4QO h long belt of Mississippian and Permian lirne- stones recording an interval when the terrane was a stable block (Gabrielse et al. 1991b). During the Middle Jurassic, the Cache Creek Terrane was thrust over the northern and eastern margins of Stikinia, depositing diagnostic fossili- ferous limestone and chert clasts from the Cache Creek Terrane into Middle to Late Jurassic conglomerates of the Bowser Basin. Similarly, the Early Jurassic Inkdin Formation of the Cache Creek Terrane contains detritus believed to be derived from the Quesnellia terrane (Monger et al. 1991). Thus, by Middle Jurassic, the Stikinia, Quesnellia, and Cache Greek terranes were at least loosely amalgamated and located next to the craton. Previous paleomagnetic studies suggest that the terranes underlying the Insular Belt (Fig. 2) may have collided with those of the Intermontane Belt by mid-Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous time to create a fairly coherent as

ic Complex marking the intervening suture (Monger et al. 1982). Subsequently, this assemblage of terranes moved north-northwesterly in panels on dominantly dextral faults beside the North American craton, reaching their present position in the Late Eocene ( - 45 Ma) (Irving et ad. 1996). Paleomagnetic data for Eocene (52 -44 Ma) rocks throughout the Canadian Cordillera, except for the Queen Charlotte Islands (Irving and Wynne 1991), show that the Cordilleran terranes have not moved significantly with respect to the North American craton since then. Local The ovate Whitehorse Pluton is exposed over 160 h2 (Fig. 3). It intrudes two members of the Late Triassic Lewes River Group. The Hancock Member comprises up to 6W m of limestones and minor siltstones, and the overlying Man- danna Member comprises up to several hundred metres of crystal-rich, volcanogenic lithic greywacke and shale with minor red, bioturbated siltstone and pebble conglomerate (Hart and Radloff 199Q). The southern part of the Whitehorse Pluton is intruded by a few narrow vertical diabase dikes of uncertain age. investigate the paleomagnetism of the Molson dikes as a function of distance from the CSBZ. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Geology Molson Dike Swarm The swarm intrudes the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province and the Pikwitonei Domain. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. The frequency of dike intrusion increases toward and within the belt. Molson dikes range from ultramafic to mafic in composi- tion. Chemically, they display characteristics of tholeiitic basalts [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975] and komatiites [Scoates and Macek, 1978] which have rift-type chemical affinities [Baragar and Scoates, 1981; Scoates, 1981]. Olivine, orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, plagioclase, and hornblende represent initial crystallization phases. Opaque minerals are mainly chromite, magnetite with ilmenite lamellae, and minor fine-grained sulphide minerals occurring as inclusions in hornblende, such as pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite, and pyrite [Scoates and Macek, 1978]. Within the Thompson Belt the Molson dikes were deformed and metamorphosed during the Trans-Hudson Orogen. The dikes southeast of the belt, however, generally escaped this event. In the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province, deuteric alteration of olivine to magnetite and serpentine occurs and varying degrees of crystal fractionation features are developed [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975]. Pikwitonei Granulite The high-grade metamorphism of the granulites is dated between 2695 + 2 Ma and 2637 + 2 Ma (U-Pb zircon [Heaman et al., 1986b]) with a metamorphic peak at -2640 ZHAI ET AL.: MULTIPLE INTRUSIONS OF THE MOLSON DIKES 21,719 Ma [Mezger et al., 1990]. The principal minerals of the granulites in the Pikwitonei Domain include clinopyroxene, plagioclase, hornblende, biotite, quartz, and magnetite. Garnet occurs locally in intermediate to mafic rocks. Olivine can also be seen locally in some ultramafic rocks. The main mineral assemblages of metamorphically retrogressed or reworked granulites in the CSBZ are characterized by garnet, quartz, biotite, amphibole, and feldspar. Incipient Paleo- proterozoic metamorphism led to destruction of magnetite in the Archean granulites via biotite-, hornblende-, or garnet- forming reactions due to aqueous fluids penetrating the granulites [Russell, 1981; Bleeker, 1990]. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. investigate the paleomagnetism of the Molson dikes as a function of distance from the CSBZ. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Geology Molson Dike Swarm The swarm intrudes the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province and the Pikwitonei Domain. Dikes found in the Thompson Belt and in the Split Lake Block are believed to be equivalent to the Molson dikes on the basis of chemical 21,717 21,718 ZHAI ET AL.' Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. Olivine, orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, plagioclase, and hornblende represent initial crystallization phases. Opaque minerals are mainly chromite, magnetite with ilmenite lamellae, and minor fine-grained sulphide minerals occurring as inclusions in hornblende, such as pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite, and pyrite [Scoates and Macek, 1978]. Within the Thompson Belt the Molson dikes were deformed and metamorphosed during the Trans-Hudson Orogen. The dikes southeast of the belt, however, generally escaped this event. In the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province, deuteric alteration of olivine to magnetite and serpentine occurs and varying degrees of crystal fractionation features are developed [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975]. investigate the paleomagnetism of the Molson dikes as a function of distance from the CSBZ. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: vision accepted May 15, 1980 The mobility of Morocco relative to Africa during the early history of the Atlantic has long been debated: arguments have been developed from Atlantic kinematic considerations and from paleomagnetic results. Both types of arguments are reexamined here. Using a new model of the Atlantic Ocean evolution described elsewhere, it is shown that the reconstructions of the positions of Africa relative to North America before the Atlantic opening, and at the times of magnetic anomalies M22 and J, do not imply a major motion of Morocco independent of Africa during these periods of time. The corresponding geomagnetic paleopoles have been recomputed from sample sites located on both "mobile" Morocco and "stable" Africa. The results indicate that the virtual geomagnetic pole of "mobile" Morocco for the Liassic falls within the 95% confidence cone of "stable" Africa. It is thus concluded that no major movement has occurred between "mobile" Morocco and "stable" Africa during the early phases of opening of the central Atlantic Ocean. target_context.excerpt: kaline rocks Regional geology The late Cretaceous alkaline ~trusions of the Eastern Desert may be divided for convenience into three groups. The first, the trachytic (boston- itic) dikes, sills and plugs (B sites) intrude into the sediments of the Ham- mamet Formation and surrounding metamorphic rocks of the basement complex in the region southwest of Quseir (Fig. 1). Several of these units have been affected by uranium mineralization and these have been studied in detail by Hussein and El Kassas (1971, 1972). In the field the rocks usually form prominent relief and are recognizable by their light colored fine-grained character. 171 The rocks are composed predominantly of alkali feldspar and subordinate

he mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of conti

asin col- lapse, and to transport of sediment towards the axial valley. Approximately 50 m.y. after the initial uplift, continental separation accompanied by tholei- itic volcanism begins. This takes no account of the subsequent spreading behaviour, that is, it is independent of the two spreading stages, proposed and discussed by Girdler and Styles (1976), Davidson and Rex (1980) and Richardson and Harrison (1976). The first, the trachytic (boston- itic) dikes, sills and plugs (B sites) intrude into the sediments of the Ham- mamet Formation and surrounding metamorphic rocks of the basement complex in the region southwest of Quseir (Fig. 1). Several of these units have been affected by uranium mineralization and these have been studied in detail by Hussein and El Kassas (1971, 1972). In the field the rocks usually form prominent relief and are recognizable by their light colored fine-grained character. 171 The rocks are composed predominantly of alkali feldspar and subordinate quartz, ferromagnesian minerals, zircon and apatite. In the absence of the radial arrangement of the feldspar laths, considered diagnostic of bostonites, it is suggested here that the rocks be called by the more familiar term, trachyte. El Manharawy (1972) quoted Rb-Sr ages for these rocks ranging from 300 m.y. to 74 m.y. despite the gross similarity of the rocks. As indicated earlier there are two phases of igneous activity, the first being volumetrically much more extensive than the second. The opening of the earlier phase was marked by the extrusion of alkaline basalts of which the Wadi Natash lavas are the best known (El Shazly and Krs, 1973), although slightly older lavas are reported from the. Wadi Amba in the northern Eastern Desert. The paleopole position of the lavas is indis- tinguishable from those obtained from the intrusions reported here. The radiometric age dates and the meagre fauna from the basal Nubian Sandstone Formation (Ward and McDonald, 1979) are consistent with a late Cretaceous age for the igneous units. The paleopole positions compare closely with those from other African rocks of similar age, on the assumption of zero relative motion between the Nubian and other African plates (Fig. 11). Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of continental rifting to the northern Red Sea. The earlier, alkaline phase of igneous activity is related to regional up- lift while the second, tholeiitic phase is associated with widening of the rift valley. I. Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation.
